topic: William Scoville & Brenda Milner (1953-1957): Patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) & Bilateral Hippocampal Anterograde Amnesia
visual_mode_reason: Patient H.M.'s selective loss of new conscious memory consolidation while keeping childhood memories and IQ intact directly maps the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus versus neocortical storage.

primary_case.title: Bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in Patient H.M. (Henry Gustav Molaison) & Milner's neuropsychological dissociation
primary_case.place: Hartford Hospital, Connecticut & Montreal Neurological Institute

people.name: Henry Gustav Molaison (Patient H.M., 1926-2008)
people.role: 27-year-old Connecticut assembly-line worker who underwent experimental surgery for intractable epilepsy and lost the ability to form new declarative memories

people.name: William Beecher Scoville
people.role: Hartford neurosurgeon who performed the bilateral 8-centimeter medial temporal lobe suction resection on August 25, 1953

people.name: Brenda Milner
people.role: Montreal Neurological Institute neuropsychologist whose decades of testing with H.M. founded modern memory neuroscience

core_facts.fact: On August 25, 1953, at Hartford Hospital, neurosurgeon William Scoville removed bilateral medial temporal lobe tissue in 27-year-old Henry Molaison to halt severe seizures that had resisted maximum anticonvulsant doses.

Scoville estimated an 8-centimeter rostrocaudal resection encompassing the anterior hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, uncus, and amygdala in both hemispheres (later refined via post-mortem histology to ~5 cm plus entorhinal cortex).
Henry's major seizures dropped dramatically and his Wechsler-Bellevue IQ actually rose from 104 preoperatively to 112-118 postoperatively because he was less sedated.

Yet from the moment he woke up in 1953, Henry suffered profound anterograde amnesia: he forgot hospital staff minutes after they stepped out of the room and re-read the same magazine endlessly without recognition.
In Scoville and Milner's 1957 report across 10 medial temporal patients, severe memory loss appeared ONLY when hippocampal removal was bilateral and extended posteriorly.
Henry retained vivid childhood memories from the 1930s and early 1940s alongside intact grammar, manners, and arithmetic, proving long-term memories are not permanently stored inside the hippocampus.

Using active rehearsal without distraction, Henry could hold a three-digit number such as 584 in working memory for 15 minutes — but the instant his attention was diverted, both the number and the test vanished.

On Brenda Milner's 28-choice stylus stepping-stone maze (1965), Henry failed to learn the full spatial path even after 215 trials, revealing how heavily spatial declarative sequences depend on the hippocampus.

Post-mortem 2,401-slice histological reconstruction after Henry's death in 2008 revealed spared posterior hippocampal tissue (~2 cm) that remained functionally disconnected because his entorhinal gateway was excised.
Across 55 years of testing, Brenda Milner had to re-introduce herself to Henry at the start of every single session.

In Brenda Milner's 1962 three-day mirror-drawing test (reported in 1968), a metal shield hid Henry's hand while he traced a five-pointed double-outline star across 30 trials (10 trials per day over 3 days) looking only in an upright mirror, dropping from roughly 30 border errors on Day 1 to just 1 or 2 errors by Day 3 with zero conscious memory of ever seeing the apparatus.

Suzanne Corkin (1968) confirmed Henry's multi-day procedural motor skill learning across rotary pursuit and bimanual tracking, proving that spared subcortical basal ganglia and cerebellar motor circuits acquire physical habits and skills independently of the hippocampus.

wow_facts.fact: Henry Molaison could hold the number '584' in his head for 15 straight minutes by whispering clever math tricks — then forget the number AND the test 30 seconds after someone changed the subject.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Working memory and long-term memory run on completely separate hardware.

wow_facts.fact: Brenda Milner studied Henry for more than fifty years, yet she was a brand-new stranger to him every single morning she walked through his door.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Without the hippocampal gateway, experience evaporates the moment attention moves.

wow_facts.fact: Henry's IQ score actually went UP to 118 after the surgery that erased his ability to remember eating lunch 30 minutes earlier.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Intelligence, personality, and vocabulary live outside the hippocampus.

wow_facts.fact: Scoville's unilateral patients kept normal everyday memory, proving one intact hippocampus can carry conscious episodic encoding, whereas losing both freezes life in the present tense.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Bilateral loss crossed an irreversible threshold.

wow_facts.fact: On Day 3 of mirror-star tracing, Henry swore he had never seen the mirror contraption in his life — then glided his pencil around all five star points with near-zero errors, proving hands and habits remember via basal ganglia and cerebellum.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Split human memory into declarative ('knowing what') and procedural ('knowing how') brain systems.

misconceptions.myth: The hippocampus is the permanent hard drive where all your life memories are stored.
misconceptions.truth: Henry kept childhood memories from decades before 1953, proving the hippocampus consolidates new memories before cortical networks store them long-term.

misconceptions.myth: Patient H.M. lost his intelligence, language, and immediate short-term span.
misconceptions.truth: His IQ measured 118 and his immediate digit span remained completely intact as long as he rehearsed uninterrupted.

misconceptions.myth: Scoville removed 100 percent of Henry's hippocampus cleanly and nothing else.
misconceptions.truth: 2014 post-mortem histology showed posterior hippocampal remnants survived, while bilateral entorhinal and perirhinal cortex removal severed its cortical input.

misconceptions.myth: Memory is one single mental faculty across the whole cortex.
misconceptions.truth: H.M. overturned single-memory dogma by dissociating hippocampal episodic memory from prefrontal working memory and basal-ganglia/cerebellar motor skill memory.

everyday_hooks: Repeating a new phone verification code under your breath across the room, getting interrupted for two seconds by a text, and realizing the digits vanished.
Remembering every lyric of a song from age twelve while forgetting why you just walked into the pantry.
Hopping onto a bicycle ten years after your last ride and balancing smoothly within two seconds through cerebellar and basal ganglia motor memory.
Meeting three people at a loud reception and losing their names thirty seconds after shaking hands because your attention jumped.
